title: The Birth of Calculus
text: The word 'calculus' comes from the Latin 'calculus', which means ‘pebble.’ Long before numbers were invented, shepherds counted their sheep using small stones: one animal, one pebble. When all the sheep had returned to the pen, the number of stones gave the exact count. Thus, arithmetic was born.

title: Writing: Preserving Information
text: The Sumerians invented cuneiform writing in Mesopotamia. For the first time, information could be permanently recorded on clay tablets rather than memorized by humans. This externalization of memory was an essential step toward data storage, one of the foundations of computer science.

title: Egyptian numerals
text: The Egyptians developed a comprehensive system for writing numbers that enabled them to count, measure, and carry out major engineering projects. The emergence of symbols dedicated to quantities marked an important milestone in the history of calculation.

title: Babylonian tablets: \n solving equations
text: Using clay tablets inscribed with cuneiform, they developed algorithmic methods for solving algebraic problems. More than three millennia before the advent of computer science, they demonstrated that computational rules could be applied systematically, foreshadowing future algorithms.

title: Euclid: The First Famous Algorithm
text: In 'The Elements', Euclid describes a systematic method for calculating the greatest common divisor of two numbers. More than two thousand years later, this algorithm is still taught and used in computer science. It perfectly illustrates that a problem can be solved by a sequence of precise instructions.

title: Invention of Zero
text: Around the 5th century in India, the mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta introduced a new symbol to represent absence. By depicting emptiness, nothingness, and the void, he finally made representable what had previously been unrepresentable. Zero thus paved the way for positional notation. Passed on to the Arab world and then to Europe, this system became the universal language of mathematics.

title: Al-Khwārizmī Invents Algorithms
text: The Persian scholar Al-Khwārizmī wrote a treatise describing systematic methods for performing calculations. His Latinized name, Algoritmi, gave rise to the word 'algorithm.' His work helped spread the Indo-Arabic numerals to the West and established the idea that a calculation can be performed by following a precise procedure.

title: Invention of the abacus
text: Building on ancient calculation techniques, the abacus became widely used in China around the 13th century. Thanks to its rows of movable beads, it allowed numbers to be represented and arithmetic operations to be performed quickly. By making quantities visible and manipulable, it marked a major milestone in the history of calculating tools and foreshadowed future calculating machines.

title: Introduction of Indo-Arabic numerals to Europe
subtitle: Leonardo Fibonacci
text: Leonardo Fibonacci published the 'Liber Abaci', a work that introduced Indo-Arabic numerals and modern methods of calculation to Europe. Simpler than Roman numerals, these new numerals revolutionized commerce, accounting, and mathematics.

title: Invention of the printing press
subtitle: Johannes Gutenberg
text: Revolutionized Europe in Mainz with the invention of movable metal type. His screw press, adapted from those used by winemakers, enabled the rapid and mass reproduction of texts. In 1455, he completed the '42-line Bible,' the first major printed book. This technology broke the monopoly of the scribal monks and democratized access to knowledge. It was the driving force behind the Renaissance and the spread of ideas across the continent. This innovation transformed the dissemination of knowledge by enabling the mass production of books and documents, thereby paving the way for a new era of communication and cultural exchange.

title: Invention of the logarithm
subtitle: John Napier
text: John Napier invented logarithms, a method that converts multiplication into addition and division into subtraction. Scientific calculations became faster, and this innovation would be used for more than three centuries. Combined with logarithmic tables and later with slide rules, they became essential tools for engineers, astronomers, and scientists before the advent of electronic calculators.

title: Invention of the slide rule
subtitle: William Oughtred
text: William Oughtred invented the slide rule by applying Napier's logarithms to simplify multiplication, division, and complex calculations. For nearly 350 years, it served as a tool for scientists, until the advent of electronic calculators. Compact and fast, it enabled calculations with remarkable precision and supported major scientific advances, from industrial engineering to the space race.

title: Invention of the Pascaline
subtitle: Blaise Pascal
text: Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline, the first mechanical calculating machine. Thanks to its gear wheels, it automated arithmetic operations and freed calculations from relying solely on human intervention. This invention marked the birth of mechanical calculation.

title: Invention of Leibniz’s mechanical calculator
subtitle: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
text: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz designed an arithmetic machine capable of multiplication. Thanks to its grooved cylinders, it stored the multiplicand and automated the calculation. Leibniz was also interested in the binary system, paving the way for the theoretical foundations of computer science.

title: Binary Calculation Explained
subtitle: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
text: Leibniz published 'Explanation of Binary Arithmetic', demonstrating that all numbers can be represented using only two digits: 0 and 1. This idea, purely theoretical at the time, showed that a simple numeral system could represent all of arithmetic and mathematical operations. Three centuries later, it would become the fundamental language of computers, where bits would be used to store and process all digital information.

title: Invention of the Jacquard Loom
subtitle: Joseph Marie Jacquard
text: Joseph Marie Jacquard, from Lyon, developed a programmable loom using punch cards. These cards controlled the fabric patterns and allowed instructions to be stored. The Jacquard loom is thus considered one of the first programmable systems, a precursor to the computer and the robot.

title: Invention of the electric telegraph
subtitle: Samuel Morse
text: Samuel Morse and other inventors developed the electric telegraph, capable of rapidly transmitting messages over long distances. Information was encoded as electrical pulses using Morse code. This invention marked the beginning of digital communications.

title: The Principle of the Analytical Engine
subtitle: Charles Babbage
text: While developing his Difference Engine, Charles Babbage conceived the Analytical Engine and incorporated punch cards inspired by the Jacquard loom. These cards would have been used to give instructions to the machine. Although never completed, this invention laid the fundamental principles of the programmable computer.

title: Invention of Morse Code
subtitle: Samuel Morse
text: Samuel Morse invented an alphabet consisting solely of dots and dashes. Each letter was converted into a sequence of electrical signals that could be transmitted over long distances. This was one of the first digital representations of information.

title: The First Computer Program
subtitle: Ada Lovelace
text: In the United Kingdom, Ada Lovelace wrote the first computer program for Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine. Her algorithm made it possible to calculate Bernoulli numbers, illustrating the power of programmed instructions and laying the foundation for modern software.

title: Boolean Algebra
subtitle: George Boole
text: The British mathematician George Boole proposed a new form of symbolic logic. He reduced human reasoning to two fundamental states: True (1) and False (0). His logical operations (AND, OR, NOT) made it possible to process binary variables through calculation. Although it had fallen into obscurity, this theory became the foundation of modern electronic circuits in 1937. Without this algebra, the architecture of today’s computers and software would not exist.

title: The Universal Machine and the Decryption of Enigma
subtitle: Alan Turing
text: A visionary pioneer of computer science and an unsung hero of World War II. In 1936, Alan Turing laid the theoretical foundations of computation with his ‘Universal Machine,’ the conceptual ancestor of all computers. At Bletchley Park, he designed and perfected the Bombe, a machine that made it possible to decipher messages encoded by Enigma, thereby making a decisive contribution to the Allied victory.

title: Application of Boolean Algebra to Circuits
subtitle: Claude Shannon
text: In his master's thesis, Claude Shannon demonstrated that Boolean algebra can be used to design electrical relay circuits. He showed that logical operations (AND, OR, NOT) can be performed using electrical switches. This discovery bridges mathematics and electronics and marks the true birth of modern digital computing.

title: First Functional Programmable Computer
subtitle: Konrad Zuse
text: Konrad Zuse built the Z3 in Germany, the first fully automatic programmable computer using electromechanical relays. Capable of executing programs stored on a punched tape, it performed complex calculations without human intervention. Although destroyed during World War II, it is still considered today to be the first operational programmable computer in history.

title: The Modern Computer
subtitle: John von Neumann
text: Mathematician John von Neumann formalized the architecture of modern computers in his report on the EDVAC. He proposed storing programs and data in the same memory, allowing the machine to easily modify the instructions it executes. This architecture, consisting of a processor, memory, and input/output devices, is still used by the vast majority of computers today.

title: ENIAC: The First Vacuum-Tube Computer
text: Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, the first general-purpose programmable electronic computer, built at the University of Pennsylvania under the direction of John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert for the U.S. Army. With its 18,000 vacuum tubes, 70,000 resistors, 10,000 capacitors, and 1,500 relays, it occupied an entire room (167 m²) and consumed 150 kW. Originally intended for calculating ballistic firing tables, it was unveiled in 1946 and marked the beginning of the era of modern electronic computing.

title: Invention of the transistor
text: J. Bardeen, W. Shockley, and W. Brattain of Bell Laboratories developed the first bipolar transistor, ushering in the era of modern electronics. Developed simultaneously in Europe as the transistron, the transistor replaced vacuum tubes and made the miniaturization of computing machines possible. It would become the foundation of computing and digital technologies.

title: Information Theory
subtitle: Claude Shannon
text: Claude Shannon publishes 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication'. He introduces the bit as the fundamental unit of information and demonstrates how to measure, transmit, and protect data from errors. His work lays the foundation for telecommunications, the Internet, and modern digital systems.

title: The Invention of the First Compiler and the Term 'Bug'
subtitle: Grace Hopper
text: A pioneer in computer science and rear admiral in the U.S. Navy. In 1952, she created the first compiler (A-0), which automated the translation of programs: a revolution that paved the way for high-level languages. In 1947, a moth trapped in the Harvard Mark II inspired the term 'bug' for a program error and the expression 'debug,' which entered common parlance thanks to her.

title: Birth of Artificial Intelligence
subtitle: Dartmouth Conference
text: In the summer of 1956, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and several other researchers gathered at Dartmouth College. They coined the term ‘Artificial Intelligence’ and envisioned machines capable of reasoning, learning, and solving problems. This conference marked the official beginning of a field of research that would profoundly transform computer science.

title: Invention of the Integrated Circuit
text: Jack Kilby and later Robert Noyce invented the integrated circuit, which combines multiple electronic components on a single silicon chip. Instead of individually assembling thousands of transistors, resistors, and capacitors, it became possible to manufacture them together. This innovation significantly reduced the size, cost, and power consumption of computers, paving the way for microprocessors, personal computers, and smartphones.

title: Invention of the BASIC language
text: John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz created the BASIC language (Beginner’s All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) to make programming accessible to students. Easy to learn, it became the language of choice for the first microcomputers of the 1970s and 1980s. Millions of people thus discovered programming thanks to BASIC.

title: Moore's Law:\n Chips Become More Powerful
text: Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel, observes that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every two years. This dramatic growth allows for a continuous increase in computer power while reducing their cost. For more than half a century, this empirical law would guide the entire semiconductor industry.

title: First Email
text: This innovation marked the beginning of email, which would become one of the most widely used communication tools in the world.

title: The Mouse, Windows, and Copy-Paste
subtitle: Douglas Engelbart
text: On December 9, 1968, Douglas Engelbart gave a live demonstration of a series of innovations that seemed to come from the future: the mouse, windows, copy-paste, collaborative editing, hyperlinks, and videoconferencing. This presentation, nicknamed 'The Mother of All Demos,' profoundly influenced Apple, Microsoft, and modern computing as a whole.

title: ARPANET: The Beginnings of the Internet
text: The U.S. Department of Defense launched ARPANET, the first network connecting multiple remote computers. The first message sent contained only the letters 'LO,' as the machine crashed before it could type 'LOGIN.' Designed to share computing resources among research centers, ARPANET introduced the principles of networked communication that would give rise to the Internet a few decades later.

title: UNIX: The modern operating system
text: At Bell Labs, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie developed UNIX, a simple, portable, multi-user operating system. Designed around small, specialized programs that could be combined with one another, UNIX profoundly influenced all of modern computing. Linux, macOS, Android, and today’s operating systems are its direct descendants.

title: Relational Databases
subtitle: Edgar F. Codd
text: British researcher Edgar F. Codd published a revolutionary model for organizing data in the form of interconnected tables. Relational databases facilitate the storage, retrieval, and updating of large amounts of information. They quickly became the foundation for banks, government agencies, businesses, and later, websites.

title: At Sign
text: Engineer Ray Tomlinson chose the @ symbol to separate the user’s name from the computer’s name in the first email addresses. A simple typographical character, the at sign quickly became the universal symbol of email. Today, it more broadly symbolizes the Internet and digital communication.

title: First Commercial Microprocessor
text: The Intel 4004 was designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor (Intel), and Masatoshi Shima (Busicom). Incorporating 2,300 transistors on a 12 mm² chip, it executed 60,000 instructions per second. Originally created to power a desktop calculator (Busicom 141-PF), it laid the foundation for all modern processors and launched the personal computing revolution.

title: C Language: \n The Foundation of Modern Computing
subtitle: Dennis Ritchie
text: Dennis Ritchie developed the C language at Bell Labs to program the Unix system. Fast, portable, and close to the hardware, it became one of the most influential languages in history. Many modern operating systems, software programs, and languages (C++, Java, C#, Python, etc.) are direct descendants of its concepts.

title: Birth of Ethernet
subtitle: Robert Metcalfe
text: Robert Metcalfe invented Ethernet at Xerox PARC to enable multiple computers to communicate within the same local area network. Initially based on a shared cable and a collision detection mechanism, this technology gradually became the global standard for computer networks. Still in use today in both businesses and homes, Ethernet is one of the fundamental building blocks of modern Internet infrastructure.

title: The Birth of Microsoft
text: In 1975, Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in Albuquerque. Their first success came from adapting the BASIC language for the Altair 8800. The company really took off in 1980 thanks to a landmark contract with IBM. It then became the global software giant with the MS-DOS system.

title: The Arrival of Computers in Homes
subtitle: Apple II
text: The first personal computer truly accessible to the general public, designed by S. Wozniak and marketed by S. Jobs at Apple. Equipped with a 1 MHz 6502 processor, 4 KB of RAM (expandable to 48 KB), color graphics (high resolution 280×192), and a built-in keyboard. Sold with an iconic beige case and the rainbow logo, it popularized BASIC, games (such as Breakout), VisiCalc (the first spreadsheet program), and brought computing into homes, schools, and small businesses.

title: VisiCalc: \n The software that sold computers
text: VisiCalc became the first electronic spreadsheet available on the Apple II. For the first time, businesses could instantly recalculate their financial spreadsheets. Many people bought a computer solely to use VisiCalc, making it the first true ‘killer app’ in the history of computing.

title: Birth of the Minitel
text: French engineers from CNET and CCETT conceived an interactive network connecting citizens to information via the telephone. Supported by the Transpac network, the Minitel gave rise to the Télétel and heralded the end of paper. A precursor to the Internet, it ushered in the era of consumer digital services in France.

title: The PC Becomes a Standard
subtitle: IBM PC
text: IBM launched its first Personal Computer (IBM PC 5150), designed to make computing accessible to businesses and individuals. Thanks to its open architecture, numerous manufacturers were able to produce compatible computers, quickly creating a vast ecosystem around the PC standard. Combined with the MS-DOS system, it established a new global benchmark that would dominate the personal computing market for years to come.

title: Computers Enter the Home
subtitle: Commodore 64
text: The undisputed king of the 1980s. With more than 12 to 17 million units sold, the 'C64' was the computer that transformed the family living room into a space for gaming and learning. Its inimitable SID sound, multicolored sprites, and rock-bottom price ($595, then quickly dropping to $200) gave rise to a generation of amateur programmers, musicians, and gamers.

title: GNU Project
subtitle: Richard Stallman
text: In 1983, Richard Stallman launched the GNU Project to create a free operating system. In response to the closure of source code, he drafted the GNU Manifesto two years later. In it, he defined the four fundamental freedoms: to use, study, modify, and redistribute. This initiative gave rise to the free software movement and the GPL license. The project would later merge with the Linux kernel to form the GNU/Linux system.

title: The Computer with a Graphical User Interface
subtitle: Macintosh
text: Apple released the Macintosh, the first personal computer to popularize the graphical user interface and the mouse among the general public. With its windows, icons, and intuitive use, it made computing more accessible. It helped establish the graphical user interfaces found on all computers today.

title: The Invention of the Web
subtitle: World Wide Web
text: At CERN, Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web to facilitate the sharing of scientific documents among researchers. He invented the three fundamental technologies of the Web: HTML pages, hypertext links, and the HTTP protocol, as well as the first browser capable of viewing them. Initially designed for the scientific community, the Web gradually transformed the Internet into a global space for the exchange of information and revolutionized access to knowledge.

title: Linux Kernel
subtitle: Linus Torvalds
text: Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old Finnish student, began developing a new operating system kernel. He posted his famous message in August, asking for feedback on his 'hobby,' which he did not expect to be 'big or professional.' In September, version 0.01 was released, consisting of just 10,239 lines of code. The GPL license was quickly adopted for the project, encouraging global collaboration. This kernel, named Linux, would become the crucial missing piece to complete the GNU system.

title: The Web Becomes Accessible
subtitle: Mosaic Browser
text: Developed at the NCSA, Mosaic was the first graphical browser to achieve widespread success. For the first time, text, images, and hyperlinks were displayed in a single, user-friendly window. Mosaic made the World Wide Web accessible to everyone and paved the way for modern browsers such as Netscape, Firefox, Chrome, and Edge.

title: The Birth of E-Commerce
subtitle: Amazon
text: Jeff Bezos founded Amazon as an online bookstore. The company demonstrated that it was possible to purchase products directly on the Internet with just a few clicks. Amazon would go on to become one of the world’s largest e-commerce players and help bring about a lasting transformation in consumer habits.

title: Wiki
text: In March 1995, Ward Cunningham launched WikiWikiWeb, the first website that could be edited by its visitors. Inspired by the Hawaiian word wiki, meaning quick, he wanted to make it easier to share programming patterns. The concept revolutionized the Web by allowing anyone to edit content without technical skills. This collaborative architecture relies on trust and peer review rather than control. Six years later, this 'wisdom of the crowd' model would serve as the foundation for the creation of Wikipedia.

title: IBM Deep Blue vs. Garry Kasparov
text: The Day the Machine Defeated the Chess King On May 11, 1997, after an intense six-game match, IBM’s Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov, the reigning world champion. This historic victory, the result of 11 years of research at IBM, proved that brute computational power could surpass human intuition in a field as complex as chess, paving the way for modern advances in AI.

title: The Emergence of Google: \n The World’s Information Is Organized
text: Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded Google based on a new algorithm for ranking web pages: PageRank. Unlike existing search engines, it measures the popularity of pages based on links between websites. Google revolutionized online information search and quickly became the world’s most widely used search engine.

title: Birth of Wikipedia
text: A universal, multilingual encyclopedia co-founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. It is a free work, meaning anyone is free to redistribute it. Managed as a wiki on the wikipedia.org website, it allows all Internet users to write and edit articles, earning it the title of a collaborative encyclopedia. Furthermore, Wikipedia is the website that best embodies the spirit of the Internet.

title: Facebook: Social Networks
text: Created by Mark Zuckerberg along with several Harvard students, Facebook allows users to create a profile, share content, and communicate with friends and family. The social network experienced explosive growth and permanently transformed online interactions. It ushered in the era of global social platforms.

title: YouTube: Video for Everyone
text: Founded by three former PayPal employees, YouTube allows anyone to upload and watch videos for free on the Internet. Within a few years, the platform became the world’s leading video library and revolutionized the dissemination of knowledge, music, and entertainment.

title: iPhone: The Modern Smartphone
text: Apple introduced the iPhone, a device that combines a cell phone, digital music player, web browser, and pocket computer into a fully touch-based interface. With its multi-touch screen and an operating system designed for mobile apps, it profoundly transformed the way people interact with digital technologies. The smartphone gradually became a true connected personal computer, used by billions of people.

title: Android: The Smartphone Operating System
text: Google launches Android, an open-source operating system for mobile phones. Adopted by numerous manufacturers, it fuels the rise of smartphones and mobile apps. Today, Android powers the majority of smartphones worldwide.

title: Bitcoin and the Blockchain
subtitle: Satoshi Nakamoto
text: Under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, an unknown author introduced Bitcoin, the first digital currency operating without a central bank. Its innovation is based on the blockchain, a distributed ledger that guarantees the integrity of transactions through cryptography. This technology would pave the way for cryptocurrencies and numerous applications of digital trust.

title: GDPR Takes Effect
text: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) strengthens European citizens’ rights regarding their personal data and imposes new obligations on businesses and organizations worldwide. A true turning point in digital governance, the GDPR is rapidly becoming a global benchmark for privacy protection.

title: The Rise of Generative AI
subtitle: ChatGPT
text: OpenAI launches ChatGPT, a conversational agent based on a large language model (LLM) capable of understanding and generating text in natural language. By enabling users to engage in dialogue, program, translate, or write content, it makes generative artificial intelligence accessible to the general public. Its widespread adoption marks a new stage in the digital revolution and is gradually transforming the way humans interact with computer tools.
